title: APIs and Data Exchange
summary: See how software exposes capabilities, validates messages, reports outcomes, and evolves contracts without surprising its consumers.
prerequisites: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for browser API examples
learningOutcomes: Describe an API as a contract rather than a URL.
Design predictable requests, responses, errors, and pagination.
Choose among request-response, GraphQL, events, and webhooks.

heroVisual.title: An API call crosses a governed boundary
heroVisual.caption: The contract covers more than the success payload.

nodes.label: Consumer
nodes.detail: Chooses an operation and supplies input.

nodes.label: Transport
nodes.detail: Carries the message, often with HTTP.

nodes.label: Response or event
nodes.detail: Communicates outcome in a documented shape.

sections.title: 1. An API is a contract between software boundaries
sections.summary: The contract defines capabilities, inputs, outcomes, and change rules.

blocks.text: An application programming interface is the agreed surface one software component uses to request behavior or data from another. The interface can be local or remote; a web API commonly uses HTTP, but HTTP alone does not make the contract understandable.

items.title: Operation
items.summary: What the consumer can ask the provider to do.

items.title: Input
items.summary: Required and optional values, types, formats, constraints, and defaults.
items.example: currency must be an ISO code

items.title: Outcome
items.summary: Success shape, errors, side effects, and timing.

items.title: Change policy
items.summary: How compatible additions, deprecations, and breaking changes are handled.

blocks.title: Contract
blocks.body: A testable agreement about behavior and data at a boundary. Documentation describes it; validation and tests enforce it.

sections.title: 2. HTTP APIs model resources and operations
sections.summary: Use HTTP semantics instead of tunneling every action through one generic endpoint.

blocks.title: REST is an architectural style
blocks.body: A JSON-over-HTTP endpoint is not automatically RESTful. The useful goal is a coherent interface that respects HTTP semantics, representations, links where helpful, cache behavior, and stateless requests.

blocks.explanation: A retried creation request can reuse a client-supplied idempotency key when the API defines that behavior.

sections.title: 3. Messages need explicit schemas and errors
sections.summary: Predictable data shapes reduce hidden assumptions between teams and systems.

blocks.explanation: Names, units, time zones, nullability, and enumerated states are part of the contract.

blocks.code:
{
  "type": "https://example.com/problems/invalid-currency",
  "title": "Currency is not supported",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Use one of USD, EUR, or CAD.",
  "instance": "/requests/req_9"
}
blocks.explanation: A structured error gives machines stable fields and people a useful explanation.

items: Document required, optional, nullable, and omitted fields separately.
Specify units, precision, character encoding, and time-zone rules.
Reject unknown or invalid values according to an explicit policy.
Use stable machine-readable error codes or types.
Never expose secrets or internal stack traces.

sections.title: 4. Authentication and authorization answer different questions
sections.summary: Identity does not automatically grant permission.

rows: May this caller perform this action on this resource?
How much work may this caller request in a period?
What security-relevant action occurred, when, and under which identity?
blocks.caption: Security controls are complementary

blocks.title: Do not place secrets in browser-delivered code
blocks.body: Anything sent to a browser can be inspected by the person controlling that browser. Keep privileged credentials in a trusted server environment.

visual.title: A protected request
visual.caption: Each control has a distinct responsibility.

nodes.label: TLS
nodes.detail: Protects data in transit and authenticates the server.

nodes.label: Authentication
nodes.detail: Establishes which principal is making the request.

nodes.label: Authorization
nodes.detail: Checks whether that principal may perform this action on this resource.

nodes.label: Validation
nodes.detail: Checks that input is structurally and semantically acceptable.

sections.title: 5. Pagination, caching, retries, and idempotency make APIs operable
sections.summary: Production behavior includes limits and failure recovery.

items.title: Pagination
items.summary: Returns bounded portions of a collection.
items.whenToUse: Use cursor pagination for stable traversal through changing ordered data.

items.title: Caching
items.summary: Reuses representations while they remain valid.
items.whenToUse: Use validators such as ETag where revalidation is useful.

items.title: Timeouts
items.summary: Bound how long a caller waits.
items.whenToUse: Set timeouts at every remote boundary.

items.title: Retries
items.whenToUse: Use backoff, jitter, limits, and idempotent behavior.
items.avoidWhen: Do not retry every status blindly.

items.title: Idempotency
items.summary: Repeated equivalent requests have the defined same effect.
items.whenToUse: Make safe retries possible for sensitive writes.

blocks.title: Retries can multiply an outage
blocks.body: A retry policy without backoff, jitter, limits, and a total deadline can create synchronized extra load exactly when a dependency is unhealthy.

items: Define maximum page size and stable ordering.
Return enough metadata or links to continue.
State which responses may be cached and by whom.

sections.title: 6. Choose the interaction style that matches the job
sections.summary: Different API styles optimize different forms of coupling and timing.

rows: Simple request-response semantics and broad tooling.
Consumers may make several requests for complex views.
Consumers select fields through a typed query schema.
Cost control, caching, and resolver behavior need deliberate design.
Provider calls a consumer when an event occurs.
Delivery, retries, signatures, ordering, and replay must be handled.
Producers and consumers can be decoupled in time.
Event evolution, ordering, duplication, and observability become core concerns.
Fast in-process calls with language-native types.
Version coupling and process boundaries differ from network APIs.
blocks.caption: API interaction styles

blocks.title: Use the smallest style that meets the real interaction
blocks.body: Do not introduce an event platform for one synchronous request, or a custom query language where a bounded resource API is enough.

sections.title: 7. Evolve contracts without silent breakage
sections.summary: Compatibility is a product promise enforced by evidence.

items.title: Classify the change
items.explanation: Additive optional fields differ from renamed or removed behavior.

items.title: Publish the contract
items.explanation: Generate or maintain a machine-readable schema where practical.
items.result: Consumers and tests share one definition.

items.title: Test consumers
items.explanation: Use contract tests, examples, and representative clients.

items.title: Deprecate visibly
items.explanation: Announce the replacement, migration, and end date.

items.title: Observe real use
items.explanation: Measure versions, fields, errors, and deprecated operations.

items: Adding a field does not break consumers that reject unknown fields.
Changing enum values or nullability can be breaking.
Behavioral changes matter even when the JSON shape is unchanged.
Version identifiers do not replace migration support.

glossary.definition: A defined interface through which software requests capabilities or data from another boundary.
A machine-readable or documented definition of a data shape and its constraints.
A defined property where repeating an equivalent operation does not create additional unintended effects.
Pagination that continues from an opaque position in an ordered result set.
An HTTP request sent by a provider to a registered consumer when an event occurs.
